findings.headline: Interest rate cuts are deferred; Bank Rate held at 3.75% with next reduction not expected until September 2027, while inflation risks are rising
findings.detail: The Bank of England paused its easing cycle in December 2025. With rates at 3.75%, no further cuts are forecast until September 2027. Meanwhile, CPI inflation stands at 2.8% and risks rising to 4.5%+ due to Middle East conflict and energy costs, with the possibility that rates may need to rise to control inflation.
findings.matters: The council faces an extended period of elevated borrowing costs. Refinancing of the council's £83.7m external debt and future capital borrowing will occur at rates unlikely to fall in the near term, with downside risk of rates rising instead.
findings.figures: Bank Rate 3.75%; next cut expected September 2027 to 3.50%; CPI 2.8% April 2026, potential to exceed 4.5%
findings.quote: A growing risk of inflation is anticipated, meaning interest rates will not be cut for some time, and may increase to counteract inflationary pressures arising from steepening energy costs.

findings.headline: External debt increased by £27 million to £83.7 million; £27 million borrowed in March 2026 for capital programme and land purchase
findings.detail: Total external debt grew from £56.7m to £83.7m. In March 2026, the council borrowed £15m for its 2026/27 capital programme and £12m for a land purchase, accounting for most of the year's debt increase. Long-term PWLB borrowing rose from £41.7m to £53.7m.
findings.matters: The council is significantly expanding its debt position while interest rates are held and unlikely to fall, directly contributing to rising financing costs and increasing the council's interest rate and refinancing risk.
findings.figures: External debt £56.7m → £83.7m (47% increase); £15m capital + £12m land purchase in March; PWLB long-term borrowing £41.7m → £53.7m
findings.quote: In total, external debt has increased in the year by £27.0m from £56.7m to £83.7m. This includes £15m of debt that was taken out in March 2026 to be used mainly for 2026/27 capital programme and £12m for a land purchase.

findings.headline: General Fund financing costs increased from 12.6% to 14.7% of net revenue in a single year, a 2.1 percentage point jump
findings.detail: The proportion of the council's net revenue consumed by interest and Minimum Revenue Provision (principal repayment) rose significantly. The council budgeted for 12.7% but achieved 14.7%, indicating costs are tracking above forecast and rising faster than revenue growth.
findings.matters: Rising financing costs reduce the proportion of revenue available for service delivery and signal that the council's debt position is becoming more expensive to maintain relative to its income base.
findings.quote: The proportion of general fund financing costs to net revenue stream has increased by 2.1% from last year to 14.7%.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Audit and Governance Committee Annual Report 2025-26 and Appendices
findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation for East Sussex creates structural uncertainty for the council, with governance and financial resilience to be monitored through 2026-27.
findings.detail: The Audit and Governance Committee has identified Local Government Reorganisation (LGR) as a key risk area, should a new unitary authority for East Sussex be progressed. The Committee will seek ongoing assurance over the council's governance arrangements, financial resilience, asset management, internal control and organisational capacity throughout any transition period, including lessons learned from other authorities undergoing LGR.
findings.matters: Any significant uncertainty over a council's future structure affects its capital planning, operational continuity, and borrowing headroom. A lender needs to understand the timeline, likelihood and implications of potential reorganisation.
findings.quote: Should a new unitary authority for East Sussex be progressed, this will remain a key area of focus during 2026 to 2027 and beyond.

findings.paper_title: Revised Setting of the 2026-27 Council Tax for Lewes Town Council Area report
findings.headline: Lewes Town Council precept was calculated incorrectly and required Full Council amendment
findings.detail: The Lewes Town Council precept contained an error in the Council Tax Report approved on 23 February 2026, requiring this revised Council Tax Resolution to be brought to Full Council for approval. The corrected figures show a Council Tax requirement of £15,531,100 with a basic Band D amount of £396.48.
findings.matters: Errors in Council Tax calculations indicate potential weaknesses in the council's financial control processes and accuracy of financial reporting, which is material to a lender's assessment of the council's financial management capability
findings.figures: Council Tax requirement: £15,531,100; Basic amount (Band D): £396.48; Special items: £6,792,891
findings.quote: This paper is being brought to Full Council as the Lewes Town Council Precept was incorrect in the Council's Council Tax Report approved on 23 February 2026.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Treasury Management 2025-26 Quarter 2 mid-year review report
findings.headline: Capital Financing Requirement revised down by £26.7m to £119.8m, reflecting contraction in capital plans
findings.detail: The CFR was set at £146.5m in the February 2025 Treasury Strategy but has been revised down to £119.8m following Q2 deferrals and lower capital spend forecasts. This 18% reduction reflects the shortfall between planned and forecast capital expenditure across both General Fund and HRA.
findings.matters: The CFR represents the council's underlying need to borrow for capital purposes; a material downward revision indicates capital ambitions are not being executed and raises questions about project delivery capability and whether financial plans remain achievable
findings.figures: CFR revised from £146.5m (approved strategy, February 2025) to £119.8m at Q2; reduction of £26.7m
findings.quote: As a result of updates for the capital expenditure deferrals and final year end outturn position, the Capital Financing Requirement (CFR) has been revised to £119.8m at Q2 compared to £146.5m in the treasury strategy (as approved in February 2025).

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Treasury Management 2025-26 Quarter 2 mid-year review report
findings.headline: Capital expenditure forecast of £55.2m is 46% below the revised budget of £103.3m, with acute slippage in HRA schemes
findings.detail: The council approved a £71.4m capital programme in February 2025, then added £22.9m deferred from 2024/25, creating a revised budget of £103.3m. The Q2 forecast is only £55.2m. HRA capital is particularly affected, forecast at £15.2m against a revised budget of £38.9m. The document notes the shortfall 'has reduced the level of borrowing required in the year, particularly for the HRA', but does not explain the cause of the deferral or when these schemes are expected to progress.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand whether capital programmes are being delivered as planned; large unexplained deferrals can signal project delivery issues, procurement delays, or cash constraints that may affect the council's financial stability
findings.figures: Q2 forecast £55.2m (GF £40.0m, HRA £15.2m) vs revised budget £103.3m (GF £64.4m, HRA £38.9m); HRA underspend of £23.7m or 61% against revised budget
findings.quote: Following September Cabinet approval, the total of schemes deferred from 2024/25 was £22.9m, resulting in a Revised Budget of £103.3m (GF £64.4m and HRA £38.9m). The current Q2 forecast of £55.2m (GF £40.0m and HRA £15.2m) for the year is significantly lower than the revised budget.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 3 - Referral from Cabinet - General Fund and Capital Programme
findings.headline: The 2026/27 budget was set in the context of government core funding reductions from a 'fair funding' review.
findings.detail: Cabinet notes that the balanced budget for 2026/27 was prepared following a government 'fair funding' review that reduced the council's core funding allocation. The document provides no detail on the scale or duration of this reduction, but the decision to use capital receipts for revenue suggests it is material.
findings.matters: A reduction in core Government funding is material to financial sustainability—a lender needs to know if this is a one-off or recurrent and what actions the council plans to absorb it.
findings.figures: Reduction quantum not specified; Council Tax increased 2.99%, resulting in Band D charge of £242.02 for 2026/27.
findings.quote: The recommended balanced budget for 2026/27, was set in the context of the reduction in core funding arising from the Government 'fair funding' review.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 3 - Referral from Cabinet - General Fund and Capital Programme
findings.headline: Council is using flexible capital receipts to fund revenue costs, which Cabinet acknowledges is not its preferred approach.
findings.detail: The Cabinet approved a Flexible Use of Capital Receipts Policy for 2025/26 and 2026/27, explicitly noting this is not their preferred method of funding revenue but necessary ahead of Local Government Reorganisation. This represents the council turning to non-recurring capital resources to balance its revenue budget, indicating underlying pressure on revenue funding.
findings.matters: Using capital receipts to fund ongoing revenue costs is structurally unsustainable—a lender needs to understand whether this is temporary or reflects a permanent shortfall in revenue funding capacity.
findings.figures: Specific amount of capital receipts to be used for revenue not stated in this document.
findings.quote: the proposed 'Flexible Use of Capital Receipts Policy', was not the Cabinet's preferred way to fund revenue costs but was prudent to have in place in the lead up to Local Government Reorganisation.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Section 25 Statement of S151 Officer
findings.headline: HRA business plan sustainability flagged as uncertain due to rent policy and inflation volatility
findings.detail: While the 2026/27 HRA budget is balanced, the S151 Officer explicitly states that future HRA projections warrant review due to uncertainties in rent policies, inflation, and the sustainability of the HRA business plan itself. The officer recommends close monitoring and proactive adjustments.
findings.matters: The HRA is a material part of council finances and borrowing; uncertainty about its long-term viability could require significant business plan changes, service reductions, or additional borrowing.
findings.figures: HRA general reserves £1.9m; 2026/27 HRA budget balanced
findings.quote: However, future projections warrant review due to uncertainties in rent policies, inflation, and the sustainability of the HRA business plan. Close monitoring and proactive adjustments to the business plan are recommended.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Section 25 Statement of S151 Officer
findings.headline: Funding gap of £0.99m in 2027/28 widening to £1.76m by 2029/30, further worsened by recent government settlement changes
findings.detail: The S151 Officer identifies a trajectory of deteriorating funding. The government's Final Local Government Settlement, announced 9 February 2026, made last-minute changes that added an extra £200k per year to the pressure on top of the already-projected gaps. The council is developing savings measures to address this multi-year challenge.
findings.matters: Growing government funding gaps that accelerate across the medium term indicate unavoidable service cuts or efficiency savings are ahead, raising questions about the sustainability of current service levels and the council's trajectory.
findings.figures: £0.99m gap 2027/28; £1.76m gap 2029/30; £200k additional annual pressure from recent settlement changes
findings.quote: projected funding gaps of £0.99m for 2027/28 rising to £1.76m by 2029/30. These funding gaps are already expected to increase by circa £200k per year as of a result of last-minute changes to the Final Local Government Settlement announced on 9th February 2026.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Section 25 Statement of S151 Officer
findings.headline: Reserves forecast at £2.036m, meeting minimum but not optimal level, reducing financial headroom
findings.detail: The S151 Officer recommends maintaining £2m minimum unallocated reserves, aiming for £4m optimal with a £5m ceiling. The 2026/27 forecast is £2.036m—just barely above the minimum and £2m below the optimal level. The officer explicitly notes this leaves no room for managing contingencies and underscores the need for careful stewardship.
findings.matters: Thin reserves significantly limit the council's capacity to absorb unexpected pressures or revenue shortfalls, reducing financial resilience and increasing risk to creditors and lenders.
findings.quote: The forecasted reserve for 2026/27 is £2.036m, which just meets the minimum requirement but does not reach the optimal level, underscoring the need for careful stewardship.
